comments.text:
Personally, I don't mind if my QR code feeds all my basics into the system (including PAMI and even my full history) while I still have a few items to answer about THis visit!  What people hate, in my experience, is being forced to constantly re-enter stuff that is in 8 billion computers about me, in fact it's everywhere EXCEPT healthcare.

So I envision walking up with my QR and saying "Here's me" ["bleep! got it"], and now here's why I'm here (the non-standardized-yet questionnaire questions.

author.headline: Co-Founder @ BulkSched · Automating medical appointment scheduling inside Epic · Building for CIUSSS du Québec and provincial health systems across Canada

comments.text: July 2026 as a hard deadline — interesting. On the scheduling side of care, we're seeing the same friction: CIUSSS admin teams still juggling between Epic and Excel because native tools don't speak batch. That's exactly what we're building BulkSched around — SMART on FHIR, launched from Hyperspace. The clipboard is usually just a symptom of a workflow that has no native surface in Epic.

author.name: Gary Meyer
author.headline: Health Tech Strategy & Decision Architecture | AI & Interoperability at Scale | Bridging Healthcare & Technology

comments.text:
This is a great step forward—especially moving from PDFs to structured data that can actually show up in workflow.

You can already see the next layer in how you describe it:
share → persist → review → then decide what becomes “active.”

The data is finally getting to the right place,
but the criteria that determine what happens next still live somewhere else.

Curious how you see that evolving—so the same information that reduces intake friction can also reduce the downstream back-and-forth that happens after submission.

author.name: Mary Jane Bogacki
author.headline: Certified Coding Specialist (CCS)

comments.text:
I suspect that outdated patient bios in neglected health apps would cause a lot of workflow disruption and eventually cause providers to sideline patient provided documents. However, provider-generated requests for specific data, prior to a visit, would allow a patient to consider and consent ahead of time.
The health history data is the most likely to be objective and up to date, and (as soon as/as long as other providers scrutinize their documentation for scribe hallucinations) then interoperability continues to be the bottleneck.
